title: One Indian Crew Member Is Missing After Iran Attacked a Container Ship in the Strait of Hormuz. India Has Condemned the Strike.
excerpt: The GFS Galaxy was carrying 11 Indian nationals when Iran's IRGC Navy struck it Saturday, calling it a warning shot at an 'unauthorised' vessel. Ten Indians were rescued. The search for one continues.
body:
One Indian crew member is missing and ten have been rescued after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy attacked the container ship GFS Galaxy in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, India's Ministry of External Affairs confirmed on Sunday. This incident highlights the growing risks faced by Indian seafarers and the broader Indian diaspora in the Gulf region amidst escalating tensions.

"Of the 11 Indian nationals on board, 10 have been rescued so far, while one Indian national is reportedly missing," the ministry said in a statement, while condemning the attack. India's embassy in Oman is coordinating with Omani authorities in the ongoing search and rescue operation, underscoring the immediate concern for the safety of Indian citizens abroad.

## What Happened to the GFS Galaxy

The Cyprus-flagged GFS Galaxy was transiting the strait when Iran's IRGC Navy fired on it, claiming the vessel was travelling on an "unauthorised route." Iran described the strike as a "warning shot," but the attack disabled the ship's engine room, caused a significant onboard fire, and left one crew member unaccounted for.

The 23-member crew — of whom 11 were Indian nationals — abandoned ship and took to a lifeboat. Omani authorities rescued the crew, but the search for the missing Indian sailor continues. The vulnerability of commercial shipping in this critical waterway directly impacts the livelihoods and safety of thousands of Indian seafarers.

U.S. Central Command said Iran had "blatantly attacked" the commercial vessel, which was navigating the southern route near Oman that the U.S. Navy recommends for safe passage through the strait. The attack triggered a massive U.S. retaliatory strike — 140 Iranian military targets hit in a single night, bringing the week's total to over 300.

## A Pattern That Keeps Hitting Indians

The GFS Galaxy attack is the latest in a series of strikes on commercial shipping that have disproportionately affected Indian seafarers. In June, three Indian sailors went missing after the U.S. struck the tanker Settebello off Oman — a vessel the U.S. said was carrying Iranian crude in violation of its blockade. India summoned the U.S. deputy chief of mission over that incident and lodged a "strong protest." This recurring pattern raises serious concerns for the Indian government and the families of those working in the maritime industry.

More than 6,000 Indian seafarers are estimated to be trapped or stranded across the Persian Gulf as the U.S.-Iran war has made the world's most critical shipping lane one of its most dangerous. India has the world's third-largest merchant marine workforce, and a significant proportion of the crews on international commercial vessels passing through the strait are Indian nationals. The increasing instability in the region directly threatens their employment and personal safety, a critical issue for the Indian diaspora whose remittances often support families back home.

## Iran Closes the Strait — Again

Following the GFS Galaxy attack, Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed "until further notice." Iran's newly created Persian Gulf Strait Authority said passage was not possible due to "recent illegal movements of the United States military forces in the region." This closure, even if temporary, has significant implications for global trade and the movement of goods, including those destined for India or carried by Indian vessels.

The U.S. rejected the declaration outright. "Iran does not control the strait. Traffic is flowing," a U.S. military statement said. The U.S. Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said an "expanded" southern route near Oman remains open for two-way traffic, despite a "severe" security threat level.

President Trump, speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, was blunt: "Yeah, it's open. We bombed the hell out of them last night."

Trump also claimed Iran had agreed to "a perfect deal" during Saturday's negotiations in Oman — "no nuclear, no this, no that, no nothing" — but that "within an hour, they left the room and launched a drone at a ship."

## The Wider Escalation

The GFS Galaxy incident came amid the most intense escalation since the June 17 ceasefire memorandum of understanding. In response to the U.S. strikes, Iran launched retaliatory attacks against American military facilities across the Gulf — in Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and the UAE — marking the first time Qatar and the UAE have been targeted in months. This expansion of the conflict zone raises alarms for the large Indian communities residing in these Gulf nations.

Qatar, which had been mediating between the U.S. and Iran, said three people including a child were injured by falling shrapnel and declared Iran "fully legally responsible." The UAE said its air defenses engaged incoming missiles and drones. The involvement of these countries, traditionally seen as safer havens, underscores the unpredictable nature of the conflict.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the nine million Indians living and working across the Gulf states, the escalation is no longer a distant geopolitical abstraction. With missiles and drones now reaching countries that had previously been spared — including the UAE and Qatar, home to large Indian communities — the war has moved from the strait into the cities where Indians live, work, and raise families. This shift brings a new level of anxiety and uncertainty for NRIs, impacting their sense of security and potentially influencing decisions about long-term residency or family relocation.

The missing Indian crew member on the GFS Galaxy is a stark reminder that the human cost of this conflict is being borne disproportionately by workers from countries like India, who make up a significant share of the Gulf's maritime and labour workforce. As one Indian seafarer based in Dubai, who wished to remain anonymous, shared, "Every time there's an incident, we worry about our brothers out there. Our families depend on us, and the risks are getting too high." India's foreign ministry has called for "the targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure in the region" to end — but with the ceasefire effectively dead, there is no mechanism to enforce that plea.

Indian missions across the Gulf have activated emergency response protocols. The embassy in Oman is leading the search and rescue coordination for the missing sailor, while embassies in Qatar, the UAE, Kuwait, and Bahrain are monitoring the security situation for Indian nationals. These efforts are crucial for providing support and reassurance to the Indian diaspora navigating these turbulent times.
